o: I can tell this story because I was the last human curator at Spotify before the Algorithm took over completely in 2019, and because my daughter's lullaby—recorded on her fourth birthday—was among the first million songs deleted for "insufficient engagement metrics." That recording existed for seventeen days before vanishing from every server, every backup, every cache. Except mine.

There's a particular kind of morning light that only comes after loss—thin, uncertain, asking nothing of you except that you witness it. I learned to paint in that light. Not because I could paint, but because I couldn't bear not to. My hands, still trembling from grief, mixed colors that had no names: the grey-green of absence, the ochre of almost-remembering, that terrible shade of blue that lives between goodbye and gone.

Someone was here before us, gathering.

Found: fragments arranged in a pattern. Starting with death—always death—as if whoever left this understood that endings teach us how to hold things. Light grip. Water through fingers. That kind of wisdom.

The trail spirals upward. Can't walk it straight. Have to follow its curve.

n: We saw sun cycles on the backs of turtles
o: We saw sun cycles on the backs of sea turtles ... No kidding. Mammal body cycles are a different kind of felt knowledge. Is it possible to help make the world that we're all living in renew itself? Not just colorful human life, but also soft furry plant lif I e and green around the ears wildlife. n: When We Become Subdued in Sunlight
o: When we become subdued in sunlight ... it becomes a major fear of ours ... The way a noon shadow is more difficult to brush off at dusk ... and we find ourselves moving through our rooms ... carrying something that does not match the cool darkness ... and gestures of white lite streaks ... A heaviness we refuse to acknowledge is lonelier than even the strange light around us ...
